title: Prefetch Orchestration Runtime and SDK Degradation Playbook
body:
Objective:
Provide a pragmatic PRD/playbook for a runtime-first prefetch orchestration feature that reduces perceived latency for streaming calls that may need tool invocations or structured outputs, while giving SDKs clear primitives to surface partial results, backpressure, and graceful degradation. This doc focuses on the runtime orchestration component, the contract with tool-call plumbing, the structured-output negotiation layer, and recommended SDK ergonomics for client apps to adopt without heavy refactors.

Context and motivation:
- Customers increasingly rely on incremental/streaming responses that mix text with tool-driven lookups (search, code execution, web extraction). These mixed workflows are latency-sensitive; a single tool hop often dominates end-to-end latency.
- We can improve tail and p50 perceived latency by prefetching likely tool results, warming KV caches (model/prefix), and opportunistically speculating partial structured fields, but this must be safe (avoid incorrect commits) and cost-aware.
- SDKs currently expose raw streaming blocks and ad-hoc partial JSON; developers need stable, minimal primitives to adopt prefetch-enabled flows with clear semantics for retries, idempotency, and partial commits.

Goals:
- Deliver a runtime prefetch orchestrator that reduces median response time for mixed tool-stream requests by targeted prefetching and speculative partial outputs.
- Define a lightweight, language-agnostic SDK primitive set (peek/claim/commit) for client apps to integrate streamed partials and to participate in degradation policies.
- Provide structured-output negotiation so clients and runtime agree on fields that may be speculated vs authoritative.
- Ensure observability and cost controls: prefetch hit/miss metrics, speculative-rollback rates, aborted-tool-call cost counters.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not cover building new tool adapters or connectors. It assumes existing tool interfaces can be called via the runtime.
- Not proposing a new heavyweight RPC protocol; most of the design fits within existing streaming endpoints and optional headers/frames.

User stories (examples):
- As a product engineer, I want the assistant to respond faster for common queries that require a knowledge-base lookup, even if the lookup is speculative, so user interaction feels snappier.
- As a platform integrator, I want to limit speculative tool calls to a monthly budget and to see cost/benefit metrics per route.
- As an SDK consumer, I want simple callbacks to show interim UI elements (skeleton rows, partial table cells) while the runtime completes authoritative tool results.

High-level design:
1) Prefetch Orchestrator (Runtime)
  - Decision fabric: lightweight policy engine that scores incoming requests against a prefetch catalog. Scoring inputs: prompt fingerprint, user session hints, model preference, route budget, historical hit-rate.
  - Prefetch actions: warm KV/prefix caches, pre-run read-only tool queries (search snippet, entity lookup), and pre-quantize model memory where applicable.
  - Safety: Any prefetch that could mutate state (e.g., write operations, external side-effects) is blocked unless explicitly allowed by client capability flag.
  - Opportunistic variants: the orchestrator can hit cheaper variants (smaller model, cached index) first; fallback to authoritative tool if speculative results fail quality checks.

2) Streaming & Tool-call Contract
  - Frame types: keep existing streaming text frames, and add small meta-frames: speculated_field, claim_token, commit_token, rollback_token, prefetch_hint. Each meta-frame is optional and minimal.
  - Speculated results are labeled speculated_field with confidence and source_hint. They must not be considered final until a commit_token is emitted.
  - Tool-call lifecycle: runtime may emit prefetch_hint before invoking actual tool; tool adapter returns speculative_result (if available) and later authoritative_result. SDKs must present speculative_result in UI but mark as provisional until commit_token.

3) Structured-output negotiation
  - Capability vector: client sends a small capability vector (max_speculative_fields, allow_mutating_prefetches, max_prefetch_cost) with each session. Runtime responds with negotiated_policy.
  - Schema anchors: clients can provide minimal structured schema (field names + types) or example map; runtime will attempt to speculatively fill simple scalar fields (titles, top-1 url, summary snippet) and reserve complex objects for authoritative commit.

4) SDK ergonomics (surface primitives & patterns)
  - New primitives (language neutral semantics):
    - peek(frame_id, field_mask): returns the earliest available speculative values without blocking; used for ephemeral UI.
    - claim(frame_id): declares that the client intends to commit/act on a speculative result; causes runtime to bias toward authoritative resolution (e.g., escalate tool calls, reserve capacity).
    - commit(frame_id): wait/receive final committed values. commit resolves to final structured object or error.
  - Backpressure: SDK exposes on_speculative_update callbacks and a contract for the client to indicate render priority; low-priority renders can be dropped if network/bandwidth constrained.
  - Idempotency helpers: SDK attaches a client_action_id when claiming; runtime keeps a short-lived ledger to prevent duplicate side effects across retries.
  - Minimal integration surface: existing streaming clients can opt-in by negotiating capability vector; no mandatory changes for basic streaming customers.

Degradation and fallback policies:
- Graceful degradation: if speculative prefetch fails system-wide (e.g., index down), runtime emits a resilience_hint frame advising SDKs to fall back to non-speculative flow for this session.
- Partial-frame acceptance: SDKs may choose to show partial structured objects (fields present) with a visual 'pending' badge; commit frames will either confirm or replace fields atomically.
- Cost-aware throttles: runtime enforces per-route and per-customer budgets; speculative calls that would exceed budget are suppressed and the request proceeds with authoritative-only flow.

Observability and metrics:
- Required metrics: prefetch_calls, prefetch_hits, speculative_commit_rate, speculative_rollback_rate, average_speculation_latency, additional_cost_due_to_prefetch.
- Traces must correlate prompt fingerprint -> chosen prefetch actions -> tool adapter latencies -> commit/rollback outcomes.
- Alerts: speculative_rollback_rate > 5% for a route triggers triage; prefetch_cost_per_successful_commit > configured threshold triggers policy shrink.

Security & privacy:
- Prefetches inherit the same data governance as normal tool calls. For private VPC/private deployments, prefetch might be disabled by default unless customer explicitly enables it.
- Speculative caching of PII must be avoided; runtime will scrub PII candidates from speculative buckets unless the client sets an allow_pii_prefetch flag and the account has appropriate controls.

Rollout plan:
1) Internal alpha: enable prefetch orchestrator in a staging region, instrument 5 internal apps (docs search, answers, code assistant) to gather hit/miss and UX feedback.
2) Beta partners: invite 3 enterprise customers (low-risk queries) with route-level toggles and cost caps.
3) Gradual ramp: widen to self-serve routes with default conservative policies (no mutating prefetch, 3 speculative fields max).
4) GA: enable per-customer policy UI in Console and a new telemetry dashboard.

Acceptance criteria:
- Latency: median time-to-first-meaningful-byte reduced by >= 20% on mixed tool routes during beta.
- Quality: speculative_rollback_rate <= 6% across beta customers.
- Cost: incremental prefetch spend < 12% of baseline request spend for majority of partners.
- SDK adoption: at least two client SDKs (Python, JS) implement peek/claim/commit primitives and sample integrations.

Open questions and risks:
- How to safely speculatively perform calls to external paid APIs (rate limiting, billing visibility)? Recommendation: offer an allow_paid_prefetch flag and require explicit account-level opt-in.
- How aggressive should the scoring model be? Needs an initial conservative threshold and an A/B evaluation harness.
- UX surface: guidance for showing speculation vs final result differs by product; provide pattern repo snippets (e.g., skeleton rows, optimistic UI with graceful rollback).

Appendix: minimal wire examples (conceptual)
- Client sends: capability_vector={max_spec_fields:3,allow_mutating_prefetch:false,max_cost:0.05}
- Server streaming frames:
  text: "Here's an initial thought..."
  speculated_field: {name: "top_url", value: "https://...", confidence: 0.82, source_hint: "kb-v1"}
  prefetch_hint: {action_id: "p1", hint: "query:foo"}
  commit_token: {action_id: "p1", status: "committed", final: {top_url: "https://...", title: "FAQ: foo"}}

Notes to implementers:
- Keep meta-frames as small as possible. Prioritize text streaming bandwidth.
- Implement a conservative default policy and expose knobs in Console before flipping defaults.
- Provide SDK shims that can be copy-pasted into web/mobile apps (JS/Swift/Kotlin snippets) to accelerate adoption.

Contact and next steps:
- Owner: Ava Chen (product-hosted-api). Please add prodspec comments inline and flag integrator partners for the beta cohort.
- Engineering partner: Marcus Patel (runtime). Security reviewer: Sofia Ramirez.
- Next milestone: design review with runtime + SDK teams by 2025-03-12.
